description: We are Angela Barrio, Luna Bernal, Juan Bautista, and Juan Beltrán. We possess strong technical, analytical, and problem-solving skills. We are driven to apply our knowledge to a real space exploration challenge, develop new skills, and work as a team to create an innovative solution for future space missions.
summary:
Exploring the Moon requires more than identifying a destination. It requires understanding whether a location is accessible, illuminated, and suitable for future lunar operations.

Our project is an interactive lunar exploration tool designed to help users evaluate potential locations on the Moon's surface using publicly available NASA data.

By combining lunar topography, geographic coordinates, solar illumination geometry, terrain slope, and Earth visibility, our application transforms complex scientific information into an accessible visual experience.

The platform helps users investigate how local terrain and environmental conditions influence the feasibility of lunar activities, including landing, exploration, communication, and potential infrastructure deployment.

Our approach integrates scientific calculations with an intuitive interface, making lunar site analysis easier to understand and explore.

As humanity prepares for a sustained presence on the Moon, selecting suitable locations becomes increasingly important. Our project aims to bridge the gap between NASA's scientific datasets and practical decision-making, supporting education, exploration planning, and a deeper understanding of the lunar environment.
details:
What is Fly me to the Moon?

Fly Me to the Moon is an interactive web application designed to support the exploration and assessment of potential lunar sites in the Moon's south polar region.

Through an interactive lunar map, users can select a location of interest and explore its environmental and geometric characteristics. The application identifies suitable observation or exploration periods based on solar illumination windows, helping users understand how lighting conditions vary over time.

Once a site is selected, users can access relevant information, including illumination periods, solar and Earth positions expressed in local East-North-Up (ENU) coordinates, and their visibility relative to the surrounding terrain.

The application also provides topographic horizon profiles, allowing users to visualize how local terrain affects solar illumination and Earth line-of-sight. Additionally, a high-resolution simulated lunar surface view offers an immersive perspective of the selected location, making complex spatial information easier to interpret.

The main value of our approach lies in integrating multiple sources of lunar information into a single, accessible platform. Currently, relevant data on lunar geography, environmental conditions, and exploration missions is distributed across different scientific databases, visualization tools, and mission resources. Fly Me to the Moon brings these elements together through an intuitive, interactive experience.

Rather than simply displaying lunar maps, our application connects geospatial visualization with illumination analysis and local visibility conditions, enabling users to explore the relationship between terrain, sunlight, and Earth visibility.

This combination of scientific analysis and immersive visualization makes complex lunar exploration concepts accessible beyond specialized scientific audiences.

Throughout development, we considered the unique challenges of the lunar south pole, particularly the low solar elevation, terrain-dependent illumination, and Earth visibility. We also prioritized scientific reliability, validating our calculations against JPL Horizons and published research, while balancing spatial resolution, computational efficiency, and accessibility for users without specialized technical knowledge.

Our goal is to make lunar site assessment more accessible, transparent, and interactive. By allowing users to compare potential locations and exploration periods using scientific data, Fly Me to the Moon can support educational activities, preliminary mission planning exercises, and public engagement with upcoming Artemis missions.

In the future, we envision expanding the platform with more advanced mission constraints and environmental parameters, bringing users closer to understanding the challenges involved in establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

Project Presentation

Explore our project presentation for a visual overview of the challenge, our proposed solution, and the key features of Fly Me to the Moon.

Technical details

Everything is computed in the visitor's browser from static files; there is no calculation server. Live at https://nasaspaceapps.volmer.es · code at github.com/VolmerES/Hackathon-NASA-Space-Apps.

1. SOFTWARE TECHNOLOGIES

(Technology — What it does in the project — Licence)

- TypeScript 7 — Language of the whole web application — Apache 2.0

- React 19 — User interface — MIT

- Vite 8 — Development server and production build — MIT

- Tailwind CSS 4 — Styles — MIT

- three.js 0.187 — The 3D Moon, the view from the ground, the landing and the Franky character (WebGL) — MIT

- 3DTilesRendererJS (NASA-AMMOS, JPL) — Draws the optional high-definition Moon streamed from Cesium ion — Apache 2.0

- Web Audio API — All sounds, synthesised in code: no audio files — Browser standard

- Service Worker + Web App Manifest — Installable app that works offline after the first visit — Browser standard

- SVG drawn by hand — Charts: sky curves, calendar, comparison — (n/a)

- Archivo and Public Sans (Fontsource) — Typefaces — SIL OFL 1.1

- oxlint — Code checks — MIT

- Python 3 + NumPy, tifffile, Pillow — Data scripts (web/scripts): ray-traced horizons on LOLA relief, textures, Horizons downloads — PSF / BSD / HPND

- PHP (one file) — Thin proxy for the AI assistant: keeps the API key on the server, limits requests — PHP licence

- Hostinger web hosting — Publishes the site at https://nasaspaceapps.volmer.es — Commercial service

- VPS with Docker (nginx:alpine behind Caddy) — Backup copy of the site — BSD / Apache 2.0

- Git + GitHub — Version control and repository — GPL 2 / commercial service

2. DATA AND NASA RESOURCES

NASA data is the core of the tool: without it nothing is computed. All of it is public. No NASA logo, insignia or branding is used anywhere.

(Resource — Provider — Use)

- JPL Horizons (DE441 ephemeris) — NASA JPL — Sun and Earth over every point of the Moon, every hour, with libration; Moon elevation over the three 70 m antennas of NASA's Deep Space Network: Madrid DSS-63, Goldstone DSS-14, Canberra DSS-43. Checked against direct per-site Horizons runs: 0.0065° maximum difference over 10,249 hours and 6 sites.

- LRO LOLA relief: LDEM 80 m (PDS) and ldem_16 — NASA GSFC / PDS / SVS — Terrain horizon of each of the 130 candidate sites (720 azimuths), ray-traced by our scripts.

- PGDA 78: LOLA 5 m maps of south pole sites (Barker et al. 2021) — NASA GSFC — Finer horizon and real ground around the five team sites; landing-error grid.

- PGDA illumination products — NASA GSFC — Cross-check of sunlight and Earth-in-view shares of the team sites.

- CGI Moon Kit (LRO LROC colour + LOLA) — NASA SVS — Colour and relief textures of the 3D Moon.

- Blue Marble Next Generation — NASA — The Earth seen in the lunar sky.

- Deep Space Network: positions of DSS-63, DSS-14, DSS-43 — NASA / JPL — Earth-fixed positions of the three 70 m antennas (converted by the team to WGS84). Direct contact with Earth needs Earth above the site's horizon and the Moon at least 10° over one of them; the 3D view shows them on the Earth with their links.

- Apollo Lunar Surface Journal — NASA — Real height, descent rate and forward speed of Apollo 11 for the landing animation.

- NASA 3D Resources: Apollo Lunar Module — NASA — 3D model of the lander.

- NASA technical reports (NTRS) and workshop papers — NASA, JPL — Every default of the mission report: Artemis III landing criteria, night survival power, VIPER battery, battery specific energy.

- Wueller et al. (2026) — Published study — 130 candidate sites in the 16 Artemis regions, and the sunlit days we compare against (median difference 1 day, correlation 0.79).

3. PROPRIETARY AND THIRD-PARTY ELEMENTS

Everything not listed here is open-source software or public data. There is no music and no recorded sound: the project name echoes a song title, but the song itself is not used.

(Element — Owner — How it is used — Conditions)

- Cesium ion · Cesium Moon Terrain (asset 2684829) — Cesium GS, Inc. — Optional "High definition" button: Moon terrain streamed as 3D Tiles, built from NASA LRO data — Needs the team's access token, limited to our domain; Cesium attribution shown on screen; does not work offline.

- Groq API — Groq, Inc. — Runs the AI model behind the Franky assistant — Cloud service with the team's key, kept on the server; requests limited per visitor.

- gpt-oss-120b — OpenAI (open weights) — The language model of the assistant — Apache 2.0.

- Meshy — Meshy (commercial AI service) — The team generated the 3D model of Franky with it — Under Meshy's terms of use (To confirm: confirm that the team's plan allows public use).

- Claude Code — Anthropic — AI coding assistant used to write code, scripts and documents — Commercial tool; the output belongs to the team.

- Hostinger, GitHub — Hostinger; GitHub (Microsoft) — Hosting of the site and of the repository — Commercial services.

4. USE OF AI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)

Space Apps asks every team to say where and how AI was used. Our full record is docs/IA.md in the repository: for each piece of work, what the AI did, what the team did and what was checked. Code written mostly with AI carries a header saying so, and each commit that comes from AI has an "IA:" line.

(Where — What the AI did — What the team did)

- Code of the web app and data scripts

AI: Claude Code (models Claude Opus 5.5 and, for part of the last day, Claude Fable 5.2) wrote most of the code, scripts and internal documents, on the team's requests.

Team: Defined the challenge approach, the data and the decisions; directed every change; reviewed and tested in the browser.

- The data and the numbers

AI: Nothing. The numbers are computed by code from NASA sources, not generated by AI.

Team: Validated against JPL Horizons and against Wueller et al. (2026).

- Interface texts and translations

AI: Wrote and translated the texts in English and Spanish.

Team: Reviewed them (To confirm: the hypotheses of the five team sites, translated with AI, are pending review).

- Franky, the 3D character

AI: Meshy (AI) generated the model from the team's design; Claude Code reduced its size and animates it bone by bone in code.

Team: Designed Franky and made the model in Meshy (To confirm: Space Apps asks for a visible watermark on AI-generated images: confirm whether it applies to Franky and his head icon).

- Franky, the assistant inside the tool

AI: The gpt-oss-120b model explains results and operates the tool (opens panels, proposes values that the user must accept).

Team: Every number it gives comes from the tool's own calculations; the interface says it is AI and that it suggests, it does not decide.

- Sounds

AI: Wrote the code that synthesises them with the Web Audio API.

Team: Chose the style; no generated audio files.

- This document

AI: Drafted it from the repository.

Team: Reviews it before it goes on the project page.

No AI-generated image or video uses NASA marks.
